'''Norman Arthur Routledge''' (7 March 1928 – 27 April 2013) was a [[British people|British]] [[mathematician]] and [[schoolteacher]].<ref name="mathshistory">{{cite web| url=http://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Routledge.html | title=Norman Arthur Routledge | work=MacTutor History of Mathematics archive | publisher=[[University of St Andrews]] | accessdate=15 April 2020 }}</ref><ref name="obituary">{{cite news| url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/obituaries/norman-routledge-inspirational-teacher-and-mathematician-8635050.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220621/https://www.independent.co.uk/news/obituaries/norman-routledge-inspirational-teacher-and-mathematician-8635050.html |archive-date=21 June 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live | title=Norman Arthur Routledge: Inspirational teacher and mathematician | first=Tam | last=Dalyell | date=29 May 2013 | newspaper=[[The Independent]] | accessdate=15 April 2020 }}</ref> He was a personal friend of fellow mathematician [[Alan Turing]] (1912–1954).

==Life and career==
Norman Routledge was born near [[Alexandra Park, London|Alexandra Park]], north [[London]], England.<ref name="obituary" /> He was about to begin secondary education at [[Glendale County School]], [[Wood Green]], in 1939, when the outbreak of [[World War II]] intervened. He was evacuated with his mother, going to live in [[Letchworth]] with an aunt, and attending [[Letchworth Grammar School]], where he was taught mathematics by George Braithwaite.<ref name="mathshistory"/>

In 1946 Routledge matriculated with a scholarship at [[King's College, Cambridge]], where he read [[mathematics]]. He was supervised by [[Albert Ingham]] and [[Philip Hall]]. He gained a [[first class degree]] in 1949 and went on to research in [[recursion theory]]. It resulted in the papers ''Ordinal recursion'' (1953) and ''Concerning definable sets'' (1954).<ref name="mathshistory"/>

Routledge taught as a scientific officer at the [[Royal Aircraft Establishment]], [[RAE Farnborough]]. He went on to the [[National Physical Laboratory (United Kingdom)|National Physical Laboratory]] (NPL), [[Teddington]]. These were placements to fulfil the requirements for his compulsory [[Conscription in the United Kingdom#After 1945|national service]]. At the NPL in 1952 he was able to become an operator of an early version of the [[Automatic Computing Engine]]: the [[Pilot ACE]] project supported by [[Harry Huskey]]'s prototype [[assembly language|assembler]].<ref name="obituary" /><ref>{{cite book |last1=Turing |first1=Dermot |title=Prof: Alan Turing Decoded |date=2015 |publisher=History Press |isbn=978-0-7509-6524-8 |page=238 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QhxmCgAAQBAJ&pg=PT238 |language=en}}</ref>

Returning to academia, Routledge became a research Fellow in mathematics at King's College, Cambridge. He taught college undergraduates, and after a time was a director of studies.<ref name="obituary" /><ref name="mathshistory"/> In 1957, he was photographed by [[Antony Barrington Brown]]. The photograph is now in the collection of the [[National Portrait Gallery, London]].<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.npg.org.uk/collections/search/person/mp135236/norman-routledge | title=Norman Routledge (1928-2013), Mathematician and teacher at Eton College | publisher=National Portrait Gallery, London | location=UK | accessdate=15 April 2020 }}</ref>

In 1959, [[Robert Birley]], Headmaster at [[Eton College]], asked Routledge for a recommendation of some promising student for a mathematics teaching post; and he suggested himself. He taught mathematics at the school for some years and was later a housemaster. He was considered an inspirational teacher,<ref name="obituary" /> teaching among other Etonians [[Simon P. Norton]], [[Timothy Gowers]] and [[Stephen Wolfram]].<ref>{{cite web| url=https://writings.stephenwolfram.com/2019/08/a-book-from-alan-turing-and-a-mysterious-piece-of-paper/ | title=A Book from Alan Turing… and a Mysterious Piece of Paper | date=27 August 2019 | work=Stephen Wolfram Writings | first=Stephen | last=Wolfram | author-link=Stephen Wolfram | accessdate=15 April 2020 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web| url=https://blogs.ams.org/blogonmathblogs/2019/09/23/wolfram-blogging/ | title=Wolfram Blogging | date=23 September 2019 | first=Rachel J. | last=Crowell | work=AMS Blogs | publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]] | accessdate=15 April 2020 }}</ref><ref>Copeland et al., p. 44.</ref> Later in his life, he taught music for the [[Salvation Army]] community in [[Bermondsey]], southeast London.<ref name="obituary" />

Routledge was a raconteur, including on his personal life.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLVV0r6CmEsFy0scpmp2JOe87muCf5O1dg | title=Norman Routledge (Teacher) | work=Web of Stories – Life Stories of Remarkable People | publisher=[[YouTube]] | accessdate=15 April 2020 }}</ref> In retirement towards the end of his own life, he was able to be more openly gay.<ref name="obituary" />

In Turing's biography, Routledge is described as "clever, flamboyant and sometimes outrageous".<ref>''Prof:Alan Turing Decoded'', by Dermot Turing, published 2016, ISBN 978 1 84165 739 4, page 178.</ref>

==Association with Alan Turing==
Routledge was a friend of the mathematician and codebreaker [[Alan Turing]], whom he met after World War II, when Turing was in Cambridge to study physiology.<ref name="mathshistory"/> Turing wrote personal letters to Routledge towards the end of his life. After his arrest and before his trial, he sent the following cryptic [[syllogism]] to Routledge in 1952:<ref>{{cite web| url=https://kcctreasures.com/tag/norman-routledge/ | title=LGBT History Month in King's Library | date=14 February 2019 | work=King's Treasures – Special Collections of King's College, Cambridge | publisher=Library and Archives of [[King's College, Cambridge]] | accessdate=15 April 2020 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web| url=https://genius.com/Alan-turing-letter-to-norman-routledge-1952-annotated | title=Letter to Norman Routledge | date=1952 | first=Alan | last=Turing | author-link=Alan Turing | website=Genius | accessdate=15 April 2020 }}</ref><ref>Leavitt, pp. 5, 269.</ref><ref>Turing, D., pp. 246–7.</ref>

{{cquote|Turing believes that machines think<br/>Turing lies with men<br/>Therefore machines cannot think}}

The 1992 documentary programme ''The Strange Life and Death of Dr Turing'' had Routledge as one of the interviewees.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Strange Life and Death of Dr Turing (1992) |url=https://www2.bfi.org.uk/films-tv-people/4ce2b7bb5b2fb |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200704004641/https://www.bfi.org.uk/films-tv-people/4ce2b7bb5b2fb |url-status=dead |archive-date=4 July 2020 |website=BFI |language=en}}</ref>
